books.section: Topic 7.6 World War I: Home Front
United States and World War I (1914-1921)
The Progressive Era and World War I (1900-1920)

primary_sources: Harry R. Hopps, "Destroy This Mad Brute" poster, 1917

stimulus.text: The poster shows a huge gorilla wearing a German spiked helmet marked "MILITARISM." The gorilla holds a bloody club marked "KULTUR" in one hand and carries a woman in the other arm. It steps onto ground marked "AMERICA." Large lettering reads: "DESTROY THIS MAD BRUTE / ENLIST / U.S. ARMY." The poster was drawn by Harry R. Hopps in 1917.
stimulus.source_note: Poster by Harry R. Hopps, 1917, public domain (Library of Congress).

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, Harry R. Hopps poster, 1917, public domain
stem: A historian would most likely use this poster as evidence that wartime propaganda

options.text: gave Americans a fair picture of German military strength
options.misconception: A gorilla with a bloody club is a cartoon of fear, not a fair picture of an army.

options.text: used fear to build support for the war at home
was aimed mainly at German Americans living in the Midwest
options.misconception: The poster calls on Americans to enlist; it is not addressed to German Americans.

options.text: failed to persuade Americans to support the war
options.misconception: Background from the books: the poster is one of many, and the war effort drew millions of men; one poster cannot show failure.

rationales.A: A gorilla with a bloody club is a cartoon of fear, not a fair picture of an army.
rationales.B: The monster, the captive woman, and the word "America" under its feet are built to frighten viewers into enlisting.
rationales.C: The poster calls on Americans to enlist. It is not addressed to German Americans.
rationales.D: Background from the books: the poster is one of many, and the war effort drew millions of men; one poster cannot show failure.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what the poster is for. It is a recruiting poster, made to move people to act.
2. Ask how it moves them. Fear does the work: a monster stepping onto America.
3. Ask what a historian can claim from it. It shows the method, not the result.
Remember: a poster is evidence of what its makers tried to do, not proof that it worked.
